Car Culture · Lancia HF · 1953–2026

The Little Red Elephant

AMG was two engineers in an old mill. BMW M was a corporate subsidiary with thirty-five staff. Lancia's performance division began as a members' club for people who had bought six Lancias — and then a communications director's son founded the racing team behind his own company's back.

By Jolice Franklyn · Carveyance · 13 min read

Every performance badge is a promise, and most of them are making the same one. AMG, M, RS, GTI, SVT, Type R, Nismo, Quadrifoglio — the promise is this one is quicker, delivered in initials, in a typeface chosen by a committee.

Then there is Lancia HF, which is two letters and a small red elephant, running.

Consider what everyone else picked. Ferrari took a prancing horse. Lamborghini took a raging bull. Peugeot took a lion. Alfa Romeo took a serpent eating a man, which is its own conversation. Porsche took an actual coat of arms. Jaguar, showing restraint, took a jaguar.

Lancia surveyed the entire animal kingdom, considered aerodynamics, agility, ferocity and grace — and chose a cartoon elephant. In red. Sometimes four of them at once.

It is the single least intimidating thing ever bolted to a car that won six consecutive World Rally Championships, and once you know where it came from, it becomes the most intimidating.

Part oneHigh Fidelity means exactly what it says

HF stands for High Fidelity. Not high frequency, not high flow, not some retrofitted engineering acronym invented later by a marketing department that got embarrassed. Fidelity in the older, better sense: faithfulness. Loyalty.

Loyalty to Lancia, specifically — because HF did not begin as a racing badge at all. It began as a club.

At the 1960 Geneva Motor Show, a group of Lancia owners founded the Lancia Hi-Fi club. It was not a fan club. There was an entry requirement, and it was ludicrous: to join, you had to have bought at least six brand-new Lancias.

Not six cars. Six new Lancias. Over a lifetime, purchased at full price, from a company that in 1960 was expensive, technically eccentric and not remotely mass-market. That is not brand loyalty. That is a vow.

The club's own statutes survive, and they are wonderfully un-corporate. The stated purpose was to bring together motorists who had shown their loyalty to Lancia over time, and to strengthen the bonds of empathy and esteem between the members and the marque.

Empathy and esteem. Other manufacturers ran a loyalty program. Lancia founded a small emotional republic and issued it a coat of arms.The Lancia Hi-Fi club, 1960

Then "Hi-Fi" got shortened to HF, the two letters started appearing on the sportier road cars — the Flaminia Pinin Farina Coupé, the Flaminia Sport Zagato, the Flavia Coupé — and the badge quietly escaped the clubhouse.

What happened to it next is the part nobody tells you.

Part twoFebruary 1963: the team that was founded behind the company's back

Here is where every other performance-division origin story quietly loses.

In the early sixties, Lancia's technical director was Antonio Fessia — a serious, brilliant, doctrinaire engineer whose fingerprints are on the Flavia and the Fulvia, and whose view of motorsport was that it was a waste of the company's time and a great deal of the company's money.

Fessia was not wrong about the money. He was completely wrong about everything else, and one person at Lancia was in a position to do something about it.

Cesare Fiorio was the son of Sandro Fiorio, Lancia's director of communications. He was young, he was a competent driver himself, and he was — by every account since — one of those people who appears to have been born already thinking in stage times, service schedules and inexpensive ways to embarrass better-funded rivals.

In February 1963, Fiorio and a group of drivers and enthusiastic owners founded a racing team. They named it HF Squadra Corse, borrowing the initials straight from the owners' club.

And they founded it outside the company. Deliberately. As a private venture, specifically so that it would not be acting against the wishes of Lancia's own technical director.

Read that again

Lancia's works rally team — the operation that would go on to win eleven manufacturers' championships and define an entire era of the sport — was created as a workaround. It was set up by the PR chief's son, staffed partly by customers, and constituted as a private club precisely so that the head of engineering could not shut it down.

AMG was two engineers who quit and rented a mill. That is a great story. This one is a coup.

The debut came at the Rally dei Fiori at Sanremo, in 1963. Six Lancia Flavia Coupés finished in the top six places.

That is not a promising first outing. That is walking into a restaurant, ordering the entire menu, and leaving with the silverware.

Part threeFour elephants, not one

The team needed a logo, and what Fiorio chose is not the badge you know.

The original HF Squadra Corse mark was uppercase white HF letters on a black field, with four red elephants running across them, and SQUADRA CORSE beneath in white on a red bar.

Four. Not one. A small herd of red problems, approaching at speed.

The single elephant we associate with the badge today is the later, simplified version. For the team's first decade the mark was a stampede — which, given what the elephant was supposed to mean, was arguably the more honest design.

Part fourWhere the elephant came from, and why nobody is entirely sure

The animal predates the team by a decade, and its origin sits — in Lancia's own careful phrasing — somewhere between legend and reality.

The story goes that around 1953, Gianni Lancia — son of founder Vincenzo, and the company's managing director from 1949 to 1955 — adopted the little elephant as a lucky charm. He was running Lancia's ambitious and expensive works racing effort at the time, so a lucky charm was not an unreasonable thing to want.

The meaning attached to it is the good part, and it is not what you would guess. The elephant was not chosen for strength, or size, or for trampling the opposition.

It was chosen because of this: once an elephant starts running, it is very nearly impossible to stop.

That is a piece of racing logic so Italian it barely needs translation. Not we are the quickest. Not we have the most power. Just: we have started, and now you have a problem.

There are two more layers on top, both of which Lancia itself repeats.

The first is that the galloping elephant appears to draw on Eastern symbolism, in which an elephant depicted with its trunk stretched forward represents good luck and victory. Look at the badge. The trunk is forward. That detail is deliberate, and it is why every faithful reproduction of the logo gets it right.

The second is softer, and Lancia's heritage archive is careful to flag it as uncertain: some tellings attribute Gianni Lancia's affection for the elephant to a comic strip he loved reading to his children.

Which may be true, may be family memory, may be somebody at a long dinner in Turin saying "no, no, I know the real story." The archive's position is that the origin cannot be confirmed — only that Fiorio, his companions and the Hi-Fi association all adopted the same lucky charm.

A perfectly documented mascot would feel German. A Lancia mascot should involve a child, a legend, a foreign mythology, a racing team, and at least one question nobody can answer.On the pleasures of an unresolved origin

One documented detail worth keeping: the elephant was not always red. It was initially depicted in blue, and only later became the red version everyone now recognizes.

Part five1966: the letters and the elephant finally meet

So there are two separate objects moving through the early sixties. The letters, born in a 1960 owners' club, appearing on Flaminias and Flavias. And the elephant, born around 1953 as one man's superstition, adopted by a racing team in 1963.

They are fused, permanently and famously, in 1966 — on the Fulvia Coupé HF.

That car is the origin point of everything that follows. Piero Castagnero had designed the Fulvia Coupé in 1965; the HF version stripped it for competition. Bumpers deleted. Aluminum hood, doors and trunk lid. Plexiglas side and rear glass. Bare steel wheels, no hubcaps. A tuned 1,216 cc V4 making 88 hp.

Four hundred and thirty-five were built in 1966 and 1967. Then it got serious: the 1.3 HF with flared arches and 101 hp, and finally the 1.6 HF of 1969 — the Fanalone, named for its oversized inner headlamps, 1,584 cc, 113 hp on the road and up to 130 in works trim, at a curb weight of around 850 kg.

A note on the 1966 date

Lancia's own 1991 Delta brochure states that the HF logo and the elephant "met for the first time" in 1966 with the Fulvia. That is true of the road-car badge, but it is not the whole timeline: the HF Squadra Corse team logo had combined the letters with four elephants since February 1963.

Both statements are correct. They are describing different objects — one a factory badge on a production car, the other a racing team's mark. Period marketing copy rarely bothers with the distinction, and neither does most of the internet.

Part sixWhat the badge went on to do

The Fulvia's peak arrived in January 1972, on the Col de Turini, at night. Sandro Munari and Mario Mannucci won the Monte Carlo Rally by ten minutes and fifty seconds over Gérard Larrousse's substantially more powerful Porsche 911 S.

Lancia took the International Championship for Manufacturers that year with two rounds still to run — the last full season before the World Rally Championship existed. Fulvias won the Italian Rally Championship every year from 1965 to 1973 except one.

And then the badge kept going, through a lineage that has no real equivalent anywhere in motorsport:

Sixty-six years of HF
Red dots mark the moments the badge changed meaning
  1. c. 1953Gianni Lancia adopts a little elephant as a lucky charm. Initially blue.
  2. 1960The Lancia Hi-Fi club is founded at the Geneva show. Entry requirement: six new Lancias.
  3. 1961The HF letters appear on road cars — Flaminia Pinin Farina Coupé, Flaminia Sport Zagato, Flavia Coupé.
  4. Feb 1963Cesare Fiorio founds HF Squadra Corse — outside the company, to get around technical director Antonio Fessia. Logo: white HF, black field, four red elephants.

  6. 1966Fulvia Coupé HF. The letters and the elephant become a single production badge. 435 built.
  7. 1969Fulvia 1.6 HF "Fanalone." Also the year Fiat buys Lancia.
  8. 1972Munari and Mannucci win Monte Carlo. Lancia takes the International Championship for Manufacturers.
  9. 1974–76Stratos HF. Three consecutive world manufacturers' titles from a wedge with a Ferrari V6 behind the seats.
  10. 1983Rally 037 — the last rear-wheel-drive car ever to win the World Rally Championship, against Audi's quattro.
  11. 1985–86Delta S4. Supercharged and turbocharged at once. Group B ends beneath it.
  12. 1987–92Delta HF 4WD and Integrale. Six consecutive manufacturers' championships.
  13. 1994The last Integrale is built. The elephant goes quiet for thirty years.
  14. 2024Lancia unveils a new HF logo, timed to the release of the film Race for Glory.
  15. 2025Ypsilon HF: 280 hp, fully electric, lowered, track widened by 3 cm. Ypsilon Rally4 HF wins on debut season in the European championship.
  16. 2026Ypsilon Rally2 HF Integrale enters WRC2. The elephant is back in the World Rally Championship.

Part sevenHow everyone else's performance division was born

The claim on this page is that HF has the best origin story of any performance division in the industry. That deserves to be tested rather than asserted, so here is the field.

Where the fast badges came from
BadgeBornOrigin
Lancia HF1960 / 1963A members' club for owners of six new Lancias, whose initials were then borrowed by a racing team founded outside the company to circumvent the technical director. Mascot chosen a decade earlier as a personal superstition.
Mercedes-AMG1967Two Daimler engineers, Hans Werner Aufrecht and Erhard Melcher, quit and set up in an old mill in Burgstall. Named for both surnames plus Aufrecht's birthplace, Großaspach. Breakthrough: second overall at the 1971 Spa 24 Hours in a 300 SEL known as the Red Pig.
Abarth1949Carlo Abarth builds tuning kits and exhausts; the scorpion badge is his own zodiac sign. Genuinely charming, but a personal business rather than a factory department.
Alpina1965Burkard Bovensiepen develops a Weber carburetor conversion for the BMW 1500 and names the company after his family's typewriter firm.
BMW M1972BMW Motorsport GmbH, established as a formal subsidiary with roughly thirty-five employees under Jochen Neerpasch, hired from Ford. Effective. Corporate.
Ford RS1970Advanced Vehicle Operations at Aveley. "Rallye Sport" as a dealer and parts network. A brilliant program with an administrative birth.
Nismo1984Nissan consolidates two in-house competition departments into one subsidiary. Sensible reorganization.
TRD1976Toyota Racing Development, formalizing the older Toyota Sports Corner parts operation.

AMG is the closest rival and it is genuinely great — two employees walking out and building race engines at night in a rented mill has real romance to it. But it is still the standard shape of the story: talented people leave, start a firm, get good, get bought.

HF is a different shape entirely. Nobody left. Nobody founded a business. A group of customers made a badge, the boss's son borrowed it for a team he was not supposed to have, and the whole thing was constituted as an outside club so that the head of engineering could not veto it. The mascot arrived from a separate direction entirely, dragging a myth and a possible comic strip behind it.

The verdict

Every other performance badge was created by a company, or by people who wanted to compete with one. HF was created by people who simply loved the cars — and then quietly stolen by the racing department. It is the only performance division in the industry that started with the customers and worked its way inward.

Part eightThe elephant is running again

In March 2024, timed to the release of Race for Glory — a film about Lancia's 1983 fight with Audi — Lancia unveiled a redrawn HF logo. The colors come from the 1966 Fulvia Coupé HF. The slanted lettering comes from the 1990s Delta. The elephant sits where it always sat, trunk forward.

What followed was not a nostalgia exercise.

HF, as of 2026

280hp — Ypsilon HF, electric
212hp — Ypsilon Rally4 HF
WRC2Rally2 HF Integrale, 2026

The road car arrived in spring 2025: fully electric, 280 hp, lowered, with the track widened by three centimeters. The Rally4 HF — a 212 hp turbocharged three-cylinder with a Sadev five-speed sequential — won during its first European Rally Championship season and was still winning in 2026. Both were developed with Miki Biasion, who won two world championships for Lancia in a Delta Integrale. And in early 2026 Lancia unveiled the Ypsilon Rally2 HF Integrale for WRC2, under a newly formed works team called Lancia Corse HF.

You can be cynical about a badge revival. Usually you should be. Stellantis has form for reheating heritage, the new Ypsilon is a platform-mate of a Peugeot 208, and an electric front-wheel-drive hatchback is not a Fanalone.

But look at the actual shape of it: a competition car, in an FIA category, developed with a world champion who drove for the original team, wearing a badge that a customers' club invented in 1960 and a racing team stole in 1963, carrying an animal that a dead man's son picked out around 1953 because elephants do not stop.

Sixty-six years on, that is still the whole promise. It has never been we are the fastest.

It has always been: we have started running now.

Fact-check notes

1960 versus 1963. The badge and the team are different things with different birthdays. The HF letters date to the 1960 Hi-Fi club; HF Squadra Corse dates to February 1963. Sources that give a single founding year for "Lancia HF" are compressing two events.

The 1953 elephant. Lancia frames this as "between legend and reality," and so do we. The date, and Gianni Lancia's role, are the company's own telling rather than documented fact.

The comic strip. Stellantis Heritage explicitly notes the origin is uncertain. Treat it as folklore, not history.

Four elephants versus one. The 1963 team logo had four. The single elephant is the later simplification. Both are correct for their eras.

Blue before red. Documented by Lancia and frequently omitted everywhere else.

Manufacturers' titles. Lancia's total is usually given as ten, or eleven if the 1972 International Championship for Manufacturers is counted — which Lancia's own 1991 brochure does. Either figure is the most of any marque in the championship's history.

Ypsilon HF output. Announced at 240 hp in 2024, launched at 280 hp in 2025. Older articles still quote the lower number.

Sources: Stellantis Media releases on the HF logo (March 2024), the Ypsilon HF and Ypsilon Rally 4 HF (2024–25) and 60 years of HF passion (2025); Stellantis Heritage, "HF Squadra Corse" and "Lancia Fulvia Coupé 1.6 HF"; Lancia period sales literature, 1991; Mercedes-Benz corporate history for AMG; contemporary rally records for the 1963 Rally dei Fiori, the 1972 Monte Carlo Rally and the 1972 International Championship for Manufacturers. Current as of July 2026.
